# Domain model

The service tracks treks, the checkpoints along each trek, the participants on a trek, their check-ins at checkpoints, and the alerts raised when a participant is late. Users of the API are operations staff and administrators.

The schema is created by Flyway (`src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__init_schema.sql`). Hibernate only validates it at startup (`ddl-auto: validate`).

## Entities

Every table has the same audit columns: `created_at`, `updated_at`, `created_by` and `updated_by`. Spring Data JPA auditing fills them on every save. The times come from the injected `Clock`. The user is the username in the request's JWT, or `system` for work outside a request, such as the delay check and the seed data. Every id is a UUID generated by the application.

| Entity | Table | Fields | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `User` | `users` | `username` (unique), `password_hash` (BCrypt), `role` | Someone who can log in. Role is `ADMIN` or `OPERATIONS`. |
| `Trek` | `treks` | `name`, `start_at`, `end_at`, `status` | One departure of a trek, with its planned start and end. |
| `Checkpoint` | `checkpoints` | `trek_id`, `name`, `sequence_no`, `expected_after_hours` | A point on the trek where participants should report. `expected_after_hours` counts from the trek start. |
| `Participant` | `participants` | `trek_id`, `name`, `phone`, `emergency_contact`, `status` | A person on one trek. |
| `CheckIn` | `check_ins` | `participant_id`, `checkpoint_id`, `checked_in_at`, `recorded_by` | A participant reported at a checkpoint. `recorded_by` is the user who entered it. |
| `Alert` | `alerts` | `participant_id`, `checkpoint_id`, `status`, `acknowledged_by`, `acknowledged_at`, `resolved_by`, `resolved_at` | A participant did not report at a checkpoint in time. Its created time is `created_at`. |

The expected time at a checkpoint is `trek.start_at + checkpoint.expected_after_hours`. It is computed when needed and not stored. The alert response returns it as `expectedAt`.

## Relationships

```mermaid
erDiagram
    TREK ||--o{ CHECKPOINT : "has, in sequence order"
    TREK ||--o{ PARTICIPANT : "has"
    PARTICIPANT ||--o{ CHECK_IN : "reports"
    CHECKPOINT ||--o{ CHECK_IN : "is reported at"
    USER ||--o{ CHECK_IN : "records"
    PARTICIPANT ||--o{ ALERT : "is late in"
    CHECKPOINT ||--o{ ALERT : "is missed in"
    USER ||--o{ ALERT : "acknowledges or resolves"
```

* A trek has many checkpoints and many participants. Each checkpoint and each participant belongs to exactly one trek.
* A check-in links one participant and one checkpoint of the same trek, and names the user who recorded it.
* An alert links one participant and one checkpoint, and may name the users who acknowledged and resolved it.
* All relationships are many-to-one from the child side. Foreign keys enforce them in the database.

## State transitions

Any other change is rejected with HTTP 422.

### Trek

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> PLANNED : created
    PLANNED --> ACTIVE : needs at least one checkpoint
    PLANNED --> CANCELLED
    ACTIVE --> COMPLETED
    ACTIVE --> CANCELLED
    COMPLETED --> [*]
    CANCELLED --> [*]
```

Only an ADMIN changes trek status. Only `ACTIVE` treks are watched by the delay check and accept check-ins.

### Participant

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> REGISTERED : registered
    REGISTERED --> ON_TREK : trek must be ACTIVE
    REGISTERED --> DROPPED
    ON_TREK --> COMPLETED
    ON_TREK --> DROPPED
    COMPLETED --> [*]
    DROPPED --> [*]
```

Only `ON_TREK` participants are watched by the delay check. `REGISTERED` and `ON_TREK` participants can check in. `DROPPED` and `COMPLETED` participants cannot.

### Alert

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> OPEN : delay check raises it
    OPEN --> ACKNOWLEDGED : ops acknowledges
    OPEN --> RESOLVED : ops resolves, or the participant checks in
    ACKNOWLEDGED --> RESOLVED : ops resolves, or the participant checks in
    RESOLVED --> [*]
```

Acknowledging and resolving record the user and the time. A check-in for the same participant and checkpoint resolves an `OPEN` or `ACKNOWLEDGED` alert, and the user who recorded the check-in becomes the resolver.

## Delay rule

A participant is delayed at a checkpoint when all of these hold:

1. The trek is `ACTIVE` and its start time has passed.
2. The participant is `ON_TREK`.
3. The current time is after `trek.start_at + checkpoint.expected_after_hours + grace`. The grace period is set by `DELAY_CHECK_GRACE_MINUTES` and defaults to 0.
4. The participant has no check-in at that checkpoint.
5. The participant has no alert for that checkpoint, in any status.

Each delayed pair gets one `OPEN` alert. Rule 5 makes the check safe to repeat. It also means a resolved alert is not raised again.

## Important constraints

Constraints enforced by the database (V1 migration):

* `users.username` is unique.
* `(checkpoints.trek_id, checkpoints.sequence_no)` is unique: one checkpoint per position on a trek.
* `(check_ins.participant_id, check_ins.checkpoint_id)` is unique: one check-in per participant and checkpoint. This also stops two requests that race.
* `CHECK` constraints limit each status and role column to its enum values.
* `treks.end_at > treks.start_at`.
* `checkpoints.sequence_no > 0` and `checkpoints.expected_after_hours >= 0`.
* Foreign keys on every relationship.

Rules enforced by the services:

* Checkpoints: the expected time must fall inside the trek (422). Expected hours must grow with the sequence number (422). A used sequence number is a 409. A `COMPLETED` or `CANCELLED` trek takes no new checkpoints (422).
* Participants: no registration on a `COMPLETED` or `CANCELLED` trek (422). A phone number has 7 to 20 digits, spaces, brackets or dashes (400).
* Check-ins:
  * The checkpoint must belong to the participant's trek (422).
  * The trek must be `ACTIVE` (422).
  * The participant must not be `DROPPED` or `COMPLETED` (422).
  * The time defaults to now and must not be in the future (422).
  * A second check-in at the same checkpoint is a 409.
* Alerts: at most one alert per participant and checkpoint (delay check).

# Decisions and trade-offs

Each entry gives the decision, the reason, and what it costs.

## Architecture

**Layered Spring Boot: controller, service, repository.**
* Controllers are thin and only handle HTTP and DTOs.
* Services hold every business rule and return DTOs, so JPA entities never reach a controller or the JSON output.
* Hand-written mappers in `web/mapper` keep the conversion visible.
* Cost: services depend on the DTO package. A larger system might add a separate service model.

**Java 21, Spring Boot 3.3.13, Gradle Kotlin DSL.** The PRD allows Java 17 or 21. Java 21 is the current LTS, and records keep DTOs short.

**PostgreSQL 16 at runtime, H2 in tests, Flyway for the schema.**
* PostgreSQL is a production database and runs easily in Docker Compose.
* Flyway makes the schema versioned and repeatable. Hibernate only validates it, so a mismatch between entities and schema stops the app at startup.
* H2 in PostgreSQL mode keeps tests fast and free of Docker.
* Cost: the migrations must avoid database-specific SQL, and H2 is not a perfect PostgreSQL copy. Every write path was also checked by hand against PostgreSQL in Docker.

**UUID ids generated by the application.** UUIDs cannot be guessed or counted, need no database sequence, and let seed data use fixed, readable ids. Cost: 16-byte keys, which is no concern at this size.

## Security approach

**Stateless JWT with two roles, ADMIN and OPERATIONS.**
* `POST /api/auth/login` checks the BCrypt hash and returns an HS256 token.
* The token carries the username, the role and an expiry, with 480 minutes by default.
* `JwtAuthFilter` validates the token on each request without a database lookup.
* Stateless tokens suit a REST API and Docker scaling, and they are easy to try from Swagger.
* Cost: a token stays valid until it expires, even if the user is removed. There is no logout, refresh or revocation list.

**Role rules sit in one place, `SecurityConfig`, following the plan's role matrix.**
* Only ADMIN creates treks and checkpoints and changes trek status. That shapes the trek plan.
* Both roles read data, register participants and change their status, record check-ins, and acknowledge or resolve alerts. That is the daily operations work.
* Login, `/api/health`, Swagger and the API docs are public. Everything else needs a token.

**Login does not reveal which usernames exist.** An unknown user and a wrong password get the same message. For an unknown user, the service still runs a BCrypt comparison against a throwaway hash, so response time does not give it away.

**Secrets come from the environment.**
* `JWT_SECRET` has no default in the default profile. `JwtProperties` validates it at startup and stops the app if it is missing or shorter than 32 characters.
* Real values live in the git-ignored `.env`. Only `.env.example` is committed, with empty secrets.
* The seed passwords are demo values documented in the README.

## Scheduler approach

**`@Scheduled` with a fixed delay, in the application itself.**
* `DelayDetectionScheduler` only calls `DelayDetectionService.detectDelays()`.
* Fixed delay means the next run starts a set time after the previous one ends, so runs never overlap.
* The interval and an on and off switch come from configuration.
* This is the simplest correct choice, and the PRD leaves the approach open.
* Cost: it assumes one application instance. Several instances would each run the check. The duplicate guard below keeps that mostly harmless, but alerts could still be raised twice in a race. Running several instances would call for ShedLock or a job scheduler such as Quartz.

**The delay rule is evaluated from the data, not from missed runs.** Each run looks at the current state: overdue checkpoints with no check-in and no alert. If the scheduler was down for an hour, the next run catches up on its own.

**Time comes from an injected `Clock`.** Every service reads time from the `Clock` bean, never from `Instant.now()`. Tests use `Clock.fixed`, so the delay rule is tested at exact moments, including "exactly at the expected time is not yet late".

**A configurable grace period.** `DELAY_CHECK_GRACE_MINUTES`, default 0, delays the alert. In the field a few minutes late is normal, and the operator can tune this without a code change.

## Concurrency considerations

* **Duplicate check-ins.** The service checks for an existing check-in first and returns 409. Two requests can still pass that check together. The database unique constraint on participant and checkpoint then rejects the second insert, and the service turns that error into the same 409. The database is the final guard.
* **Duplicate alerts.** The delay check runs in one transaction on a single scheduler thread and skips any pair that already has an alert. With one instance, that is enough. A partial unique index on active alerts would also guard several instances. It was left out because H2 and PostgreSQL do not share that syntax.
* **Alert updates.** Acknowledge and resolve read the current status and change it in one transaction. Two users acting on the same alert at the same moment would both succeed, and the later write wins. There is no optimistic lock (`@Version`) yet. That is listed in `SELF_REVIEW.md`.
* **Notifications after commit.** The dispatcher listens with `@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)`, so an alert that is rolled back is never announced.

## Search implementation

**JPA Specifications with paging and a sort whitelist.**
* `GET /api/participants` takes optional `trekId`, `status`, `name` and `phone` filters. Name matching ignores case and both name and phone match partially.
* Each filter in `ParticipantSpecifications` returns a condition or null. `Specification.where(...).and(...)` skips the nulls, so any mix of filters works without hand-built queries.
* `%` and `_` in input are escaped, so they match literally and cannot widen the search.
* Results are paged, 20 by default and at most 100. The JSON shape is `content`, `page`, `size`, `totalElements` and `totalPages`.
* Sorting is allowed only on `name`, `status`, `createdAt` and `updatedAt`. Anything else is a 400 that names the allowed fields. This keeps clients off internal columns.
* Trek and alert lists use plain paging. An unknown sort field there is also a 400.
* Cost: partial `LIKE '%x%'` matching cannot use an index. That is fine at this size, but large data would need full-text search.

## Status modeling

* Each status is a Java enum stored as text. A database `CHECK` limits each column to the enum values, and the text stays readable in SQL.
* The allowed transitions live in each service as a small map from a status to the set of statuses it may move to. Anything else is a 422. The maps are easy to read and to test. See `DOMAIN_MODEL.md` for the diagrams.
* Cross-entity rules use status:
  * A trek needs a checkpoint before it becomes `ACTIVE`.
  * A participant can go `ON_TREK` only while the trek is `ACTIVE`.
  * A check-in needs an `ACTIVE` trek.
  * `DROPPED` and `COMPLETED` participants cannot check in.
* **One alert per participant and checkpoint, in any status.** This is stricter than the plan's "one OPEN or ACKNOWLEDGED alert". With the plan's rule, an alert that ops resolve by hand ("spoke to them, they are fine") would be raised again on the next run, every minute, until a check-in came in.
* **A check-in resolves the open alert for its pair.** The plan's alert flow allows this. The participant has reported, so the alert has done its job. The user who recorded the check-in becomes the resolver.

## Configuration approach

* One `application.yml` with three profiles:
  * `default` is PostgreSQL from environment variables, used by Docker Compose.
  * `local` is PostgreSQL on localhost, for runs from an IDE.
  * `test` is in-memory H2 with the scheduler off.
* Behavior that can change without a code change: `JWT_SECRET`, `TOKEN_TTL_MINUTES`, `DELAY_CHECK_ENABLED`, `DELAY_CHECK_INTERVAL_MS`, `DELAY_CHECK_GRACE_MINUTES`, `NOTIFICATION_CHANNELS`, and the database settings.
* Settings are bound to validated `@ConfigurationProperties` records (`JwtProperties`, `DelayCheckProperties`, `NotificationProperties`), so a bad value fails at startup, not later.
* The database connection wait is 5 seconds instead of Hikari's 30, so `/api/health` reports a down database quickly.

## Notification design

* **An event and pluggable channels.**
  * The delay check publishes an `AlertCreatedEvent` for each new alert. The event carries plain values, not entities, so it is safe to use after the transaction ends.
  * `NotificationDispatcher` sends it to every `NotificationChannel` named in `NOTIFICATION_CHANNELS`.
  * `LogNotificationChannel` writes a warning line, which stands in for delivery. The PRD says real delivery is not required.
* **Adding a channel is one class.** Implement `NotificationChannel` as a Spring bean, give it a name such as `email`, and add the name to `NOTIFICATION_CHANNELS`. Nothing else changes.
* **One channel cannot break the others.** A failing channel is logged and the rest still run. Unknown channel names are reported at startup.
* Cost: delivery runs on the scheduler thread with no retry. A slow real channel would need an async executor or a message queue.

## Error handling

* Every error has one JSON shape, `ApiError`, with `timestamp`, `status`, `error`, `message` and `path`. Validation errors add an `errors` map from field to message.
* `GlobalExceptionHandler` maps exceptions to statuses: 400 for validation, malformed input and bad sort, 401, 403, 404, 405, 409 for conflicts and 422 for business rules.
* Security rejections never reach a controller, so `SecurityErrorHandler` writes the same shape for 401 and 403.
* Unexpected errors return a generic 500 message. The details go only to the log.

## API documentation and health

* springdoc generates the OpenAPI document. `OpenApiConfig` adds a bearer JWT scheme, so the Authorize button in Swagger UI sends the token. Login and health are marked as open.
* `GET /api/health` is public. It returns the application name, the version from Gradle build info, the database state and the time. It answers 503 when the database does not respond, which works for container health checks.

* `GlobalExceptionHandler` maps exceptions to statuses: 400 for validation, malformed input and bad sort, 401, 403, 404, 405, 409 for conflicts and 422 for business rules.
* Security rejections never reach a controller, so `SecurityErrorHandler` writes the same shape for 401 and 403.
* Unexpected errors return a generic 500 message. The details go only to the log.

## API documentation and health

* springdoc generates the OpenAPI document. `OpenApiConfig` adds a bearer JWT scheme, so the Authorize button in Swagger UI sends the token. Login and health are marked as open.
* `GET /api/health` is public. It returns the application name, the version from Gradle build info, the database state and the time. It answers 503 when the database does not respond, which works for container health checks.

# Test notes

## Setup

You need JDK 21 to build and run tests, and Docker with Compose to run the full stack. Nothing else is required. Gradle comes with the wrapper.

```bash
cp .env.example .env
# Fill in JWT_SECRET (at least 32 characters) and DB_PASSWORD, for example:
#   JWT_SECRET=$(openssl rand -base64 48)
docker compose up --build
```

The app listens on `http://localhost:8080`. PostgreSQL is published on `127.0.0.1:5432` for database clients. Flyway creates the schema and loads the seed data on first start.

## Commands

```bash
./gradlew test                                      # all 155 tests (H2, no Docker needed)
./gradlew test --tests '*DelayDetectionServiceTest' # one test class
./gradlew build                                     # tests, Spotless check and jar
./gradlew spotlessCheck                             # formatting check (google-java-format)
./gradlew spotlessApply                             # fix formatting
docker compose up --build                           # app and PostgreSQL
docker compose down                                 # stop; add -v to also delete the database
```

## Testing strategy

All tests use JUnit 5, Mockito and AssertJ. They run against H2 in PostgreSQL mode with the real Flyway migrations, so no Docker is needed. The scheduler is switched off in the `test` profile.

| Layer | Tests | What they prove |
|---|---|---|
| Service unit tests (Mockito) | 64 | Every business rule: the delay rule, alert idempotency, check-in validation, every state transition, login, JWT, health. Repositories are mocked. Time-dependent tests use `Clock.fixed`, so "late" is tested at exact moments. |
| Controller slices (`@WebMvcTest`) | 56 | HTTP behavior with the real security config and error handler: 401 without a token, 403 for the wrong role, 400 with field errors, response shapes, paging and sort parameters, and the `ApiError` body for every error type. Services are mocked. |
| Repository and H2 tests (`@DataJpaTest`) | 21 | Real SQL on H2 against the seed data: the search filters, the unique check-in constraint, alert queries, auditing, and the full delay rule (4 alerts for the seed trek, none on a rerun). |
| Other unit tests | 10 | The JWT auditor, the notification dispatcher (channel choice, failure isolation), and the scheduler on and off switch. |
| Full application (`@SpringBootTest`) | 4 | The whole app on its own H2 database: both migrations apply, the seed users log in with BCrypt and their roles, and one flow runs through every layer. The flow covers check-in, duplicate, the delay check, the notification after commit, and acknowledge and resolve. |

Why this split: the business rules carry the risk, so they get the most tests and run fast with mocks. Slices check the HTTP contract without a database. A few H2 tests catch what mocks cannot, such as wrong SQL, missing constraints and entity and schema mismatches. One full test proves the pieces are wired together.

Every feature was also checked by hand against the Docker stack with PostgreSQL, using curl, before it was committed.

## How to test the APIs

### Seed data

| What | Value |
|---|---|
| Admin user | `admin` / `Admin@12345` (role `ADMIN`) |
| Operations user | `ops` / `Ops@12345` (role `OPERATIONS`) |
| Trek | `Kedarkantha Trek`, id `b0000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001`, `ACTIVE`, starts 2026-08-10 06:00 IST |
| Checkpoints | ids `c0000000-0000-0000-0000-00000000000{1..6}`: Dehradun 0 h, Sankri 8 h, Juda Ka Talab 28 h, Kedarkantha Summit 48 h, Sankri 72 h, Dehradun 84 h |
| Participants | Aarav Sharma `d0…01` and Diya Mehta `d0…02` are `ON_TREK`; Rohan Verma `d0…03` is `REGISTERED` |

The seed trek started in the past and is `ACTIVE`, with no check-ins. The scheduler's first run after startup therefore raises 12 alerts, one per checkpoint for each of the two `ON_TREK` participants. This shows the delay detection without any setup.

### Swagger UI

1. Open `http://localhost:8080/swagger-ui/index.html`.
2. Run `POST /api/auth/login` with `{"username":"ops","password":"Ops@12345"}` and copy the `token`.
3. Click **Authorize**, paste the token and confirm.
4. Every other endpoint now sends the token. Health and login need none.

### curl walk-through

```bash
U=http://localhost:8080
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST $U/api/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"username":"ops","password":"Ops@12345"}' | python3 -c 'import sys,json;print(json.load(sys.stdin)["token"])')
H="Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

curl -s $U/api/health                                         # public
curl -s -H "$H" "$U/api/participants?status=ON_TREK&sort=name,asc"
curl -s -H "$H" "$U/api/alerts?status=OPEN"                   # alerts raised by the scheduler

# Record that Rohan reached Dehradun (time defaults to now)
curl -s -X POST -H "$H" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' $U/api/check-ins \
  -d '{"participantId":"d0000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000003","checkpointId":"c0000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001"}'

# Acknowledge, then resolve, an alert (use an id from the alert list)
curl -s -X POST -H "$H" $U/api/alerts/<alertId>/acknowledge
curl -s -X POST -H "$H" $U/api/alerts/<alertId>/resolve

# OPERATIONS may not create treks: expect 403
curl -s -X POST -H "$H" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' $U/api/treks \
  -d '{"name":"X","startAt":"2027-01-01T00:00:00Z","endAt":"2027-01-02T00:00:00Z"}'
```

To see the delay check work from scratch, log in as `admin` and follow these steps:

1. Create a trek starting a few minutes ago.
2. Add a checkpoint at 0 hours.
3. Set the trek to `ACTIVE`.
4. Register a participant and set them to `ON_TREK`.

Within one scheduler interval, 60 seconds by default, an alert appears and the app log shows an `ALERT ...` notification line. Set `DELAY_CHECK_INTERVAL_MS=5000` in `.env` for faster feedback.

## Known limitations

* No load, performance or contract tests.
* Behavior with more than one application instance is not tested. The scheduler assumes a single instance.
* Notifications go only to the application log. Real delivery is not required by the brief.
* H2 stands in for PostgreSQL in automated tests. Every write path was also checked by hand against PostgreSQL in Docker, but that check is not automated (no Testcontainers).
* No code coverage report is generated.

# Self review

## Strengths

* **The core rule is correct and safe to repeat.** The delay check scans only `ACTIVE` treks that have started and `ON_TREK` participants. It reads time from an injected `Clock`, and it raises at most one alert per participant and checkpoint. It is tested with a fixed clock at exact moments and against the seed data on H2. In Docker, the first run raised 12 alerts and later runs raised none.
* **Data integrity sits in the database as well as the code.** Foreign keys, unique constraints and `CHECK` constraints back the service rules. A race on a duplicate check-in is stopped by the unique constraint and still returns a clean 409.
* **The API behaves predictably.**
  * One `ApiError` shape is used for every failure, including 401 and 403 from the security layer.
  * Validation errors name each field.
  * State changes that are not allowed return 422 with a clear message.
  * Unknown sort fields return 400 instead of a 500.
* **Security is stateless and simple.**
  * Tokens are JWT, and passwords are BCrypt hashes.
  * The role rules sit in one class.
  * A missing or short `JWT_SECRET` stops the app at startup.
  * Login does not reveal which usernames exist.
* **Behavior is configurable without code changes.** The scheduler interval, on and off switch, grace period, token lifetime and notification channels all come from the environment, and each setting is validated at startup.
* **Notifications are easy to extend.** A new channel is one class plus its name in `NOTIFICATION_CHANNELS`. A failing channel does not stop the others.
* **Tests and documentation.** There are 155 automated tests across services, controllers, H2 SQL and the full application. Every feature was also run by hand against PostgreSQL in Docker before its commit. `docs/ISSUES.md` records each real problem found during the build and how it was fixed.

## Weaknesses

* **There is no optimistic locking on alerts.** Two users acknowledging or resolving the same alert at the same moment both succeed, and the later write wins. Adding `@Version` to `Alert` would turn the second request into a conflict.
* **The delay check is chatty with the database.** It makes two existence queries per participant and checkpoint. That is fine for a few treks, but slow for thousands. One query per trek that returns the existing check-ins and alerts would scale better.
* **Services return web DTOs.** This keeps entities out of controllers, but ties the service layer to the API shape.
* **The search uses `LIKE '%x%'`.** Partial name and phone search cannot use an index.
* **Login has no rate limit or lockout.** BCrypt slows guessing, but nothing stops many attempts.

## Known limitations

* **Single node only.** Several app instances would each run the scheduler. Alerts could then be raised twice in a race, because the duplicate guard is a check followed by an insert, without a database constraint on active alerts.
* **Tokens cannot be revoked.** A token stays valid until it expires, 8 hours by default, even after the user is removed or changes role. There is no logout or refresh.
* **Notifications are not delivered.** They go to the application log only, run on the scheduler thread, and have no retry.
* **There are no update or delete endpoints** for treks, checkpoints or participants. The brief does not require them, but real use would need corrections.
* **A missed checkpoint keeps its alert.** If a participant reports at a later checkpoint but never at an earlier one, the alert for the earlier one remains until someone resolves it. That is deliberate, but it may be noisy.
* **H2 stands in for PostgreSQL in automated tests.** The manual checks used PostgreSQL, but they are not automated.

## What I would improve next

1. Add `@Version` to `Alert` and return 409 on a lost update.
2. Make the delay check use one set-based query per trek. Add ShedLock, or a partial unique index on active alerts, so several instances are safe.
3. Run the repository and integration tests against PostgreSQL with Testcontainers.
4. Add refresh tokens with short-lived access tokens, and rate-limit login.
5. Send notifications asynchronously with retries, and add a real channel such as email or a webhook.
6. Add update and deactivate endpoints for treks, checkpoints and participants, with the same audit trail.
7. Add a code coverage report and Spring Boot Actuator for metrics.

## AI assistance

This project was built with Claude Code, an AI coding assistant, working step by step from `docs/STEPS.md`. The owner directed each step, chose the scope and approved every commit.

The working rules in `CLAUDE.md` governed every step:

* Check each step against the PRD before writing code.
* After each change, run the full build with all tests, rebuild the Docker stack and exercise the endpoints live.
* Commit locally only after review, and push only with explicit approval.
* Log real problems in `docs/ISSUES.md`.

That log shows six problems found by those checks rather than assumed away, including a test profile that had never run and a health check that hung while the database was down.

Parts where AI-written code most deserves careful human review, and where I am least confident:

* **`SecurityConfig` and `JwtAuthFilter`.** The order of the role rules, and which paths are public.
* **`DelayDetectionService`.** The boundaries of "late", the grace period, and the decision to never raise an alert twice for the same pair.
* **`CheckInService`.** The order of the validations and the handling of a race on the unique constraint.
* **The transaction boundaries.** Specifically, the notification listener running after commit.

# indiahikes-backend-assignment-ArushNaudiyal

Backend for the Trek Operations Platform take-home assignment. It manages treks, their checkpoints, participants and check-ins. A background job detects participants who have not reported at a checkpoint in time, raises alerts, and notifies the operations team. The API is secured with JWT and two roles.

Java 21, Spring Boot 3.3, Gradle (Kotlin DSL), PostgreSQL 16, Flyway, Spring Security with JWT, springdoc-openapi, JUnit 5 and Mockito, Docker Compose.

## Documents

| Document | Contents |
|---|---|
| [DOMAIN_MODEL.md](DOMAIN_MODEL.md) | Entities, relationships, state transitions, the delay rule, constraints |
| [DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md) | Design decisions and trade-offs |
| [TEST_NOTES.md](TEST_NOTES.md) | Testing strategy, commands, how to test the APIs, limitations |
| [SELF_REVIEW.md](SELF_REVIEW.md) | Strengths, weaknesses, limitations, next steps, AI assistance |
| [docs/BE_Assignment_PRD_Latest.md](docs/BE_Assignment_PRD_Latest.md) | The assignment |
| [docs/IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md](docs/IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md) | The original design plan |
| [docs/STEPS.md](docs/STEPS.md) | Build order, one step per commit |
| [docs/ISSUES.md](docs/ISSUES.md) | Problems found during the build and how they were fixed |

## Setup

You need:

* Docker with Docker Compose, for the single-command run.
* JDK 21, only for building, testing or running outside Docker. The Gradle wrapper downloads Gradle itself.

Create your environment file from the template, then set the two secrets:

```bash
cp .env.example .env
```

* `JWT_SECRET` must be at least 32 characters, for example `openssl rand -base64 48`.
* `DB_PASSWORD` can be any password you choose.

`.env` is git-ignored. Never commit it.

## Run with Docker Compose

```bash
docker compose up --build
```

This builds the app image, starts PostgreSQL 16, waits for its health check, then starts the app. On first start, Flyway creates the schema and loads the seed data.

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| API | `http://localhost:8080/api` |
| Swagger UI | `http://localhost:8080/swagger-ui/index.html` |
| Health | `http://localhost:8080/api/health` (public) |
| PostgreSQL | `127.0.0.1:5432`, database and user `trekops`, password from `.env` |

To stop, run `docker compose down`. Add `-v` to also delete the database volume.

## Build

```bash
./gradlew build
```

This compiles the code, runs all tests, runs the Spotless formatting check and builds the jar in `build/libs/`.

## Run locally

Use this to run the app from your IDE or Gradle against the Compose database:

```bash
docker compose up -d db
DB_PASSWORD=<value from .env> ./gradlew bootRun --args='--spring.profiles.active=local'
```

The `local` profile connects to PostgreSQL on `localhost:5432` and uses a development JWT secret. Stop the Compose `app` container first if it is running, because both use port 8080.

## Authentication

* Log in with `POST /api/auth/login` and a body of `{"username": "...", "password": "..."}`.
* The response holds a JWT. Send it on every other request as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.
* Tokens last 480 minutes by default. Set `TOKEN_TTL_MINUTES` to change that.
* In Swagger UI, call login, then paste the token into **Authorize**.

| Role | Can do |
|---|---|
| `ADMIN` | Everything, including creating treks and checkpoints and changing trek status |
| `OPERATIONS` | Read treks, participants and alerts; register participants and change their status; record check-ins; acknowledge and resolve alerts |

`/api/auth/login`, `/api/health` and the Swagger pages are public. Every other endpoint needs a token.

## API overview

| Method and path | Role | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /api/auth/login` | public | Get a token |
| `GET /api/health` | public | App name, version, status, database state |
| `GET /api/treks` | both | List treks (paged) |
| `POST /api/treks` | ADMIN | Create a trek |
| `GET /api/treks/{id}` | both | Trek with its checkpoints |
| `PATCH /api/treks/{id}/status` | ADMIN | Change trek status |
| `POST /api/treks/{id}/checkpoints` | ADMIN | Add a checkpoint |
| `GET /api/participants` | both | Search: `trekId`, `status`, `name`, `phone`, plus `page`, `size`, `sort` |
| `POST /api/participants` | both | Register a participant |
| `GET /api/participants/{id}` | both | Participant with check-ins |
| `PATCH /api/participants/{id}/status` | both | Change participant status |
| `POST /api/check-ins` | both | Record a check-in |
| `GET /api/alerts?status=` | both | List alerts (paged, newest first) |
| `POST /api/alerts/{id}/acknowledge` | both | Acknowledge an alert |
| `POST /api/alerts/{id}/resolve` | both | Resolve an alert |

Every error returns the same JSON shape: `timestamp`, `status`, `error`, `message`, `path`, plus `errors` for validation failures.

## Configuration

All settings come from environment variables. Docker Compose reads them from `.env`.

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `JWT_SECRET` | none, required | Token signing key, at least 32 characters |
| `DB_USER` / `DB_PASSWORD` | `trekops` / required | Database credentials |
| `TOKEN_TTL_MINUTES` | `480` | Token lifetime |
| `DELAY_CHECK_ENABLED` | `true` | Turns the delay check on or off |
| `DELAY_CHECK_INTERVAL_MS` | `60000` | Pause between delay checks |
| `DELAY_CHECK_GRACE_MINUTES` | `0` | Minutes after the expected time before a participant counts as late |
| `NOTIFICATION_CHANNELS` | `log` | Comma-separated notification channels |

Profiles:

* `default` is PostgreSQL from the variables above, used by Docker.
* `local` is PostgreSQL on localhost.
* `test` is in-memory H2 with the delay check off.

## Tests

```bash
./gradlew test                                      # all 155 tests, no Docker needed
./gradlew test --tests '*DelayDetectionServiceTest' # one class
./gradlew spotlessCheck                             # formatting
```

The tests run on H2 with the real Flyway migrations. See [TEST_NOTES.md](TEST_NOTES.md) for the strategy and for manual API checks.

## Seed data

Flyway migration `V2__seed_data.sql` loads:

| What | Details |
|---|---|
| Administrator | `admin` / `Admin@12345`, role `ADMIN` |
| Operations user | `ops` / `Ops@12345`, role `OPERATIONS` |
| Trek | `Kedarkantha Trek`, `ACTIVE`, starts 2026-08-10 06:00 IST |
| Checkpoints | Dehradun 0 h, Sankri 8 h, Juda Ka Talab 28 h, Kedarkantha Summit 48 h, Sankri 72 h, Dehradun 84 h |
| Participants | Aarav Sharma and Diya Mehta (`ON_TREK`), Rohan Verma (`REGISTERED`) |

Passwords are stored as BCrypt hashes. These are demo credentials; change them before any real use.

The seed trek started in the past and has no check-ins. The first delay check after startup therefore raises 12 alerts, one per checkpoint for each `ON_TREK` participant. You can see them at `GET /api/alerts`, and as `ALERT` lines in the app log.

## Project layout

```
src/main/java/com/indiahikes/trekops/
  config/        security, JWT filter and properties, auditing, OpenAPI, scheduling
  domain/        JPA entities and enums
  repository/    Spring Data repositories and search specifications
  service/       business rules, delay detection, login, health
  scheduler/     the scheduled delay check
  notification/  alert event, channels, dispatcher
  exception/     exceptions mapped to 404, 409, 422 and 400
  web/           controllers, DTOs, mappers, error handling
src/main/resources/
  application.yml
  db/migration/  V1__init_schema.sql, V2__seed_data.sql
```

## AI assistance

This project was built with Claude Code, step by step, under the working rules in [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md). [SELF_REVIEW.md](SELF_REVIEW.md) describes how the AI was used and checked.

# indiahikes-backend-assignment-ArushNaudiyal

Backend for the Trek Operations Platform take-home assignment. It manages treks, their checkpoints, participants and check-ins. A background job detects participants who have not reported at a checkpoint in time, raises alerts, and notifies the operations team. The API is secured with JWT and two roles.

Java 21, Spring Boot 3.3, Gradle (Kotlin DSL), PostgreSQL 16, Flyway, Spring Security with JWT, springdoc-openapi, JUnit 5 and Mockito, Docker Compose.

## Documents

| Document | Contents |
|---|---|
| [DOMAIN_MODEL.md](DOMAIN_MODEL.md) | Entities, relationships, state transitions, the delay rule, constraints |
| [DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md) | Design decisions and trade-offs |
| [TEST_NOTES.md](TEST_NOTES.md) | Testing strategy, commands, how to test the APIs, limitations |
| [SELF_REVIEW.md](SELF_REVIEW.md) | Strengths, weaknesses, limitations, next steps, AI assistance |
| [docs/BE_Assignment_PRD_Latest.md](docs/BE_Assignment_PRD_Latest.md) | The assignment |
| [docs/IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md](docs/IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md) | The original design plan |
| [docs/STEPS.md](docs/STEPS.md) | Build order, one step per commit |
| [docs/ISSUES.md](docs/ISSUES.md) | Problems found during the build and how they were fixed |

## Setup

You need:

* Docker with Docker Compose, for the single-command run.
* JDK 21, only for building, testing or running outside Docker. The Gradle wrapper downloads Gradle itself.

Create your environment file from the template, then set the two secrets:

```bash
cp .env.example .env
```

* `JWT_SECRET` must be at least 32 characters, for example `openssl rand -base64 48`.
* `DB_PASSWORD` can be any password you choose.

`.env` is git-ignored. Never commit it.

## Run with Docker Compose

```bash
docker compose up --build
```

This builds the app image, starts PostgreSQL 16, waits for its health check, then starts the app. On first start, Flyway creates the schema and loads the seed data.

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| API | `http://localhost:8080/api` |
| Swagger UI | `http://localhost:8080/swagger-ui/index.html` |
| Health | `http://localhost:8080/api/health` (public) |
| PostgreSQL | `127.0.0.1:5432`, database and user `trekops`, password from `.env` |

To stop, run `docker compose down`. Add `-v` to also delete the database volume.

## Build

```bash
./gradlew build
```

This compiles the code, runs all tests, runs the Spotless formatting check and builds the jar in `build/libs/`.

## Run locally

Use this to run the app from your IDE or Gradle against the Compose database:

```bash
docker compose up -d db
DB_PASSWORD=<value from .env> ./gradlew bootRun --args='--spring.profiles.active=local'
```

The `local` profile connects to PostgreSQL on `localhost:5432` and uses a development JWT secret. Stop the Compose `app` container first if it is running, because both use port 8080.

## Authentication

* Log in with `POST /api/auth/login` and a body of `{"username": "...", "password": "..."}`.
* The response holds a JWT. Send it on every other request as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.
* Tokens last 480 minutes by default. Set `TOKEN_TTL_MINUTES` to change that.
* In Swagger UI, call login, then paste the token into **Authorize**.

| Role | Can do |
|---|---|
| `ADMIN` | Everything, including creating treks and checkpoints and changing trek status |
| `OPERATIONS` | Read treks, participants and alerts; register participants and change their status; record check-ins; acknowledge and resolve alerts |

`/api/auth/login`, `/api/health` and the Swagger pages are public. Every other endpoint needs a token.

## API overview

| Method and path | Role | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /api/auth/login` | public | Get a token |
| `GET /api/health` | public | App name, version, status, database state |
| `GET /api/treks` | both | List treks (paged) |
| `POST /api/treks` | ADMIN | Create a trek |
| `GET /api/treks/{id}` | both | Trek with its checkpoints |
| `PATCH /api/treks/{id}/status` | ADMIN | Change trek status |
| `POST /api/treks/{id}/checkpoints` | ADMIN | Add a checkpoint |
| `GET /api/participants` | both | Search: `trekId`, `status`, `name`, `phone`, plus `page`, `size`, `sort` |
| `POST /api/participants` | both | Register a participant |
| `GET /api/participants/{id}` | both | Participant with check-ins |
| `PATCH /api/participants/{id}/status` | both | Change participant status |
| `POST /api/check-ins` | both | Record a check-in |
| `GET /api/alerts?status=` | both | List alerts (paged, newest first) |
| `POST /api/alerts/{id}/acknowledge` | both | Acknowledge an alert |
| `POST /api/alerts/{id}/resolve` | both | Resolve an alert |

Every error returns the same JSON shape: `timestamp`, `status`, `error`, `message`, `path`, plus `errors` for validation failures.

## Configuration

All settings come from environment variables. Docker Compose reads them from `.env`.

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `JWT_SECRET` | none, required | Token signing key, at least 32 characters |
| `DB_USER` / `DB_PASSWORD` | `trekops` / required | Database credentials |
| `TOKEN_TTL_MINUTES` | `480` | Token lifetime |
| `DELAY_CHECK_ENABLED` | `true` | Turns the delay check on or off |
| `DELAY_CHECK_INTERVAL_MS` | `60000` | Pause between delay checks |
| `DELAY_CHECK_GRACE_MINUTES` | `0` | Minutes after the expected time before a participant counts as late |
| `NOTIFICATION_CHANNELS` | `log` | Comma-separated notification channels |

Profiles:

* `default` is PostgreSQL from the variables above, used by Docker.
* `local` is PostgreSQL on localhost.
* `test` is in-memory H2 with the delay check off.

## Tests

```bash
./gradlew test                                      # all 155 tests, no Docker needed
./gradlew test --tests '*DelayDetectionServiceTest' # one class
./gradlew spotlessCheck                             # formatting
```

The tests run on H2 with the real Flyway migrations. See [TEST_NOTES.md](TEST_NOTES.md) for the strategy and for manual API checks.

## Seed data

Flyway migration `V2__seed_data.sql` loads:

| What | Details |
|---|---|
| Administrator | `admin` / `Admin@12345`, role `ADMIN` |
| Operations user | `ops` / `Ops@12345`, role `OPERATIONS` |
| Trek | `Kedarkantha Trek`, `ACTIVE`, starts 2026-08-10 06:00 IST |
| Checkpoints | Dehradun 0 h, Sankri 8 h, Juda Ka Talab 28 h, Kedarkantha Summit 48 h, Sankri 72 h, Dehradun 84 h |
| Participants | Aarav Sharma and Diya Mehta (`ON_TREK`), Rohan Verma (`REGISTERED`) |

Passwords are stored as BCrypt hashes. These are demo credentials; change them before any real use.

The seed trek started in the past and has no check-ins. The first delay check after startup therefore raises 12 alerts, one per checkpoint for each `ON_TREK` participant. You can see them at `GET /api/alerts`, and as `ALERT` lines in the app log.

## Project layout

```
src/main/java/com/indiahikes/trekops/
  config/        security, JWT filter and properties, auditing, OpenAPI, scheduling
  domain/        JPA entities and enums
  repository/    Spring Data repositories and search specifications
  service/       business rules, delay detection, login, health
  scheduler/     the scheduled delay check
  notification/  alert event, channels, dispatcher
  exception/     exceptions mapped to 404, 409, 422 and 400
  web/           controllers, DTOs, mappers, error handling
src/main/resources/
  application.yml
  db/migration/  V1__init_schema.sql, V2__seed_data.sql
```
